title: Traffic signal and cabinet: backup batteries, inverter, LED heads and relays
summary: The prize at a signalised intersection is the battery backup cabinet beside the controller: four to six 12 V AGM batteries and a 1–2 kVA inverter. Also take the LED heads, load switches, relays, breakers and surge protectors. Allow half a day. Cabinets are fed from the street: never open one until the feed is proven dead. Heads are heavy and high up.

steps.text: Look first, from at least 10 m away. Check for downed or sagging wires, a leaning pole, damaged cabinets, flooding and animals. Look for overhead lines and for streetlights on the same pole: those are a separate circuit and stay off limits.
steps.warn: Never approach a cabinet, pole or signal head near a downed wire or standing in water. A fallen line can leave the whole pole live. Back off and leave it.

steps.text: Find where the cabinet gets its power: a service disconnect, a meter box on a pedestal, a pole-mounted breaker or a buried feed from a transformer. Also look for a backup inverter, solar panels or a generator inlet. Switch off and lock every source you can reach. Test the line terminals at the service disconnect with a meter you have proved on a known live source (see safety_mains_isolation). If the line side still reads voltage, the street feed is live and you cannot isolate it. If you can't find the source or prove it dead, leave the cabinet shut.
steps.warn: A street-fed cabinet can carry 120–240 V at hundreds of amps (some are 480 V). Do not open the door until the feed is proven dead.

steps.text: Test the outside. With the meter on AC volts, read between the metal cabinet and a ground rod or bare earth, and between the door handle and the ground. Both should read zero. Don't open any cabinet that reads voltage. Then open the door (cut the padlock with bolt cutters if you need to) and stand to one side.

Without touching anything, look inside: a power panel, a main breaker and terminal blocks, a plug-in rack, a battery backup feed and often a transfer switch. Test the incoming terminals on the line side of the main breaker, and the backup inverter's output, each line to neutral and to ground, proving the meter before and after. Then switch off the main and all auxiliary breakers.
steps.warn: The line side of the main breaker stays live if the feed is live, and a backup inverter can keep a cabinet live from its batteries with the grid dead. Test both before you touch.

steps.text: Battery backup cabinet: open it and look. Switch off the inverter, then open its DC breaker or isolator. Test the inverter's AC output and input terminals for voltage. Measure the battery string voltage: 4 blocks in series is about 48 V, 2 blocks about 24 V.

Split the string. Wearing eye protection and with no rings or watches, use an insulated spanner to undo the link at the middle of the string first, tape the exposed terminals, then undo the others one at a time and tape or cap each terminal. Take the inverter's DC cables off last, negative first.
steps.warn: A 50–100 Ah battery can deliver thousands of amps into a dropped tool: it will weld the tool, burn you and may blow acid. Use insulated tools and keep metal off the terminals.

steps.text: Lift the batteries out upright, one at a time, with a helper (see safety_lifting and safety_lead_acid). Each 12 V block weighs about 20–30 kg. Check each one with the meter (see test_lead_acid) and tape its terminals.
steps.warn: AGM blocks are heavy and the case can crack if dropped. Lift with your legs, never carry them one-handed, and never lift one by its terminals.

steps.text: Inverter: label every wire, then unbolt it from the shelf. Wait at least 10 minutes after it was isolated, then measure DC volts across its DC input terminals and discharge it with a resistor lead if it is above 30 V (see safety_discharge_capacitor). An inverter of this size weighs about 10–25 kg.
steps.warn: Inverter capacitors can hold a shock for many minutes after power is off.

steps.text: Controller cabinet: pull the plug-in cards out by hand once everything is proven dead: the load switches (one per signal phase), the flash transfer relays, the flasher, the conflict monitor and the controller. Pull straight out and don't force a latched card. Write the slot number on each.

Panel parts: unscrew the breakers, surge protectors, the fan and its thermostat, the radio or cellular modem and the power supply from their rails. Photograph the wiring before you undo it, then cut multi-conductor cable 30 cm from each terminal block so you keep useful lengths.

Signal heads: only take heads that you can reach safely from the ground or a short ladder, such as pedestrian heads and push-buttons on low poles. Test their terminal block with a meter again, because a head can be live from another cabinet. Open the door, take the LED module out (a few screws or clips, with two wires), and unscrew a video detection camera from its bracket if one is within reach. Then undo the terminal block and the bracket bolts. One person supports the head while the other undoes bolts. Lower it by hand or with a rope.
steps.warn: A signal head weighs 8–25 kg, its bolts are often rusted, and a head dropped from a ladder or mast arm can kill. Do not work off a ladder alone, on soft ground or in wind.

steps.text: Leave the poles, mast arms, concrete bases and buried conduit standing. A pole that has been loosened or had its load changed can fall. Remove cable only at the cabinet end by cutting it, and leave the rest.
steps.warn: Never climb a pole or mast arm, and never put a ladder against one carrying overhead lines.

notes:
## What's worth keeping and why

- **Backup batteries.** Sealed lead-acid (AGM) blocks of 50–100 Ah at 12 V, roughly 600–1,200 Wh each, held on trickle charge by the cabinet. After a long outage they may be flat or sulfated. Test and recharge before judging them (see test_lead_acid and build_battery_bank_lead_acid).
- **Inverter.** A 1–2 kVA inverter running from 24 or 48 V, with transfer switch hardware. It makes mains from a 24 or 48 V bank. Check its label and the output waveform before you trust it with electronics.
- **LED signal modules.** Round LED discs, 200–300 mm across, 5–20 W each, with their own driver for mains voltage. Red and green ones make warning lights at a gate or a night marker: they run only from mains-voltage AC.
- **Load switches.** Plug-in solid-state relays rated roughly 10–25 A at mains voltage. Check the control input type on the label before you plan around them.
- **Flash relays.** Mains relays rated 15–25 A, with plug-in bases.
- **Breakers and surge protectors.** Ready-made protection for a small power panel.
- **Fan and thermostat.** A cabinet fan with an adjustable thermostat for a workshop or battery box.
- **Cameras and radios.** Video-detection cameras are weatherproof and make perimeter cameras. Radio or cellular modems may be useful once identified (read the label for frequency and licence).
- **Push buttons.** Weatherproof pedestrian buttons are good outdoor momentary switches.

## Why the order matters

The cabinet has three possible sources: the street, the backup inverter and an inlet for a generator. Prove all of them dead, then work from the cabinet outward: the batteries and inverter first, then the plug-in cards, then the heads.

## Heads and height

Mast arms and poles are the only structure you cannot replace. If the head is more than about 3 m up, leave it unless you have a proper lift. A rope and a second person are no substitute for a platform.

## Variations

- Only some intersections have battery backup. Check the small second cabinet beside the controller.
- Older cabinets have incandescent heads and mechanical controllers. Their heads hold a 60–150 W lamp and a reflector: not worth the risk for what they give.
- Some cabinets run 480 V or 240 V three-phase. If the incoming wiring is heavier than you expected, stop.

## What to leave

- Poles, mast arms, bases and buried loop-detector wire.
- The big cabinet shell unless you have a use for a lockable weatherproof box and the means to move it.
- Controllers and conflict monitors: they are computers with no use outside their own cabinet.
